## Two health states where one is absorbing

Consider a two *health state* model in which subjects start in health state *a*
and randomly make transitions to an absorbing health state *b* at a constant
positive rate $r$ transitions per patient per year (figure 1). 

```{r}
#| fig.align = "center",
#| fig.cap = "Figure 1. Two health state model with one absorbing state"
local({
  g <- DiagrammeR::create_graph()
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_node(graph = g, label = "a")
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_node(graph = g, label = "b")
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_edge(
    graph = g,
    from = "a",
    to = "b"
  )
  # get the node ids
  nodes <- DiagrammeR::get_node_attrs(g, node_attr = "label")
  na <- which(nodes == "a")
  nb <- which(nodes == "b")
  # set layout
  g <- DiagrammeR::set_node_position(g, node = na, x = 1L, y = 1L)
  g <- DiagrammeR::set_node_position(g, node = nb, x = 2L, y = 1L)
  # set global attributes
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "fontsize",
    value = 8L,
    attr_type = "node"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "shape",
    value = "circle",
    attr_type = "node"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "color",
    value = "black",
    attr_type = "node"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "fillcolor",
    value = "white",
    attr_type = "node"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "fontcolor",
    value = "black",
    attr_type = "node"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "color",
    value = "black",
    attr_type = "edge"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "penwidth",
    value = 0.5,
    attr_type = "edge"
  )
  # name of SVG file
  svgfile <- tempfile(fileext = ".svg")
  # render it as an svg file
  DiagrammeR::export_graph(
    g,
    file_name = svgfile,
    file_type = "svg",
    width = 480L
  )
  knitr::include_graphics(path = svgfile, rel_path = FALSE)
})
```

The number of patients occupying health state *a* at time $t$, $n_a(t)$, reduces
at a rate proportional to its current value,

$$\frac{dn_a(t)}{dt} = -r n_a(t) \tag{1}$$
which has solution $\log n_a(t) = -r t + C$ where $C$ is a constant of
integration. Defining $n_a(t = 0)$ as the population of health state *a* at
time $t = 0$ gives an expression for its population at time $t$:
$$n_a(t) = n_a(t = 0) e ^ {-rt} \tag{2}$$
Equation 2 applies to processes subject to exponential decay, including
continuous processes, such as the decay of the voltage across a capacitor
in series with a resistance, and discrete processes, such as a finite population
of subjects who move from an alive state to a dead state at a constant rate.

An approach to the problem in the discrete case is to consider the transitions
between health states as a discrete Markov process in continuous time. If it is
assumed that each subject is identical and interchangeable, the 
*system state* is fully defined by the vector of health state populations. For
example, if there are 10 subjects and two health states, there are 11 possible
system states (10 in health state *a*, zero in health state *b*; nine in health
state *a*, one in health state *b*, and so on). It is also assumed that the
number of system states is countable. Transitions between health states are
assumed to happen at random times, usually at some constant overall rate, which
requires time to be modelled as a continuous variable. There is usually interest
in capturing the system state at finite time intervals (months, years etc.),
known as time cycles.

Figure 2 shows a generalized two health state model as a Markov process diagram.
Subjects who remain in the same health state over a cycle are assumed to make
transitions back to their current health state within the cycle; these are
modelled as self loops. With two health states, there are four possible
transitions: *u* and *x* are self loops, *v* allows transitions from *a* to *b*
and *w* vice-versa. The rate associated with *v* is $r$, and the rate
associated with *w* is zero if *b* is an absorbing health state.

```{r}
#| fig.align = "center",
#| fig.cap = "Figure 2. Two health state model as a Markov process"
local({
  g <- DiagrammeR::create_graph()
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_node(graph = g, label = "a")
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_node(graph = g, label = "b")
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_edge(
    graph = g,
    from = "a",
    to = "a",
    edge_aes = DiagrammeR::edge_aes(label = "u")
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_edge(
    graph = g,
    from = "a",
    to = "b",
    edge_aes = DiagrammeR::edge_aes(label = "v")
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_edge(
    graph = g,
    from = "b",
    to = "a",
    edge_aes = DiagrammeR::edge_aes(label = "w")
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_edge(
    graph = g,
    from = "b",
    to = "b",
    edge_aes = DiagrammeR::edge_aes(label = "x")
  )
  # get the node ids
  nodes <- DiagrammeR::get_node_attrs(g, node_attr = "label")
  na <- which(nodes == "a")
  nb <- which(nodes == "b")
  # set layout
  g <- DiagrammeR::set_node_position(g, node = na, x = 1L, y = 1L)
  g <- DiagrammeR::set_node_position(g, node = nb, x = 2L, y = 1L)
  # set global attributes
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "fontsize",
    value = 8L,
    attr_type = "node"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "shape",
    value = "circle",
    attr_type = "node"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "color",
    value = "black",
    attr_type = "node"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "fillcolor",
    value = "white",
    attr_type = "node"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "fontcolor",
    value = "black",
    attr_type = "node"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "color",
    value = "black",
    attr_type = "edge"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "penwidth",
    value = 0.5,
    attr_type = "edge"
  )
  # set loop directions
  g <- DiagrammeR::set_edge_attrs(
    g,
    edge_attr = "headport",
    values = "w",
    from = na,
    to = na
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::set_edge_attrs(
    g,
    edge_attr = "tailport",
    values = "w",
    from = na,
    to = na
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::set_edge_attrs(
    g,
    edge_attr = "headport",
    values = "e",
    from = nb,
    to = nb
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::set_edge_attrs(
    g,
    edge_attr = "tailport",
    values = "e",
    from = nb,
    to = nb
  )
  # name of SVG file
  svgfile <- tempfile(fileext = ".svg")
  # render it as an svg file
  DiagrammeR::export_graph(
    g,
    file_name = svgfile,
    file_type = "svg",
    width = 480L
  )
  knitr::include_graphics(path = svgfile, rel_path = FALSE)
})
```

Generalizing equation 1, the number of subjects in health state *a* at
time $s + t$ is the number at the start of the interval, $n_a(s)$, multiplied
by the exponential term; there are no transitions from *b* to *a*:
$$
n_a(s + t) = n_a(s) e^{-rt} + 0 \tag{3}
$$
Similarly, the number in health state *b* at time $s + t$ is given by the number
who move from *a* to *b* plus the number already in *b* at time $s$:
$$
n_b(s + t) = n_a(s) (1- e^{-rt}) + n_b(s) \tag{4}
$$
In matrix form, equations 3 and 4 become
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
n_a(s + t) & n_b(s + t)
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
n_a(s) & n_b(s)
\end{bmatrix} 
\begin{bmatrix}
e ^ {-rt} & 1 - e ^ {-rt}\\
0 & 1\\
\end{bmatrix} \tag{5}
$$
This is expressed more compactly as
$$S(s + t) = S(s) P(t;s) \tag{6}$$
where $S$ is the vector of health state populations and $P(t; s)$, or
$P_{ij}(t; s)$ in matrix notation, is the transition probability matrix: the
probability that a subject who is in health state $i$ at time $s$ will be in
health state $j$ at time $t$. Equation 6 provides the mechanism for computing
the health state populations after a time cycle from the populations at the
start of the cycle and a matrix of transition probabilities.

In the case where all patients begin in health state *a*, the system has the
highest probability of making a system state change at time $t = 0$. As patients
transition to health state *b* and its population increases, the probability of
system state change reduces, until it reaches zero when all patients are in 
health state *b*. The probability that the system makes a transition at time
$t$ is $\frac{\partial P}{\partial t}$. In the case of one of the two health
states being an absorbing state (equation 6), this becomes:
$$
\frac{\partial P(t; s)}{\partial t} = \begin{bmatrix}
-r e ^ {-rt} & r e ^ {-rt}\\
0 & 0\\
\end{bmatrix} =  
\begin{bmatrix}
e ^ {-rt} & 1 - e ^ {-rt}\\
0 & 1\\
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} -r & r\\0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} =
P(t;s) Q(t) \tag{7}
$$
where $Q(t)$ is known as the transition rate matrix.

The number of transitions which occur between time $s$ and $s + t$ is given by
the Hadamard product of the health state populations and the transition
probability matrix, $S(s) \odot P(t)$,
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
n_a(s) & n_b(s)
\end{bmatrix} \odot 
\begin{bmatrix}
e ^ {-rt} & 1 - e ^ {-rt}\\
0 & 1
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
n_a(s) e ^ {-rt} & n_a(s)(1 - e ^ {-rt})\\
0 & n_b(s)
\end{bmatrix} \tag{8}
$$
where $n_a(s) e^ {-rt}$ is the number of transitions along edge *u*, 
$n_a(s) (1 - e ^ {-rt})$ along *v* and $n_b$ along *w*.

## Arbitrarily complex models

Kolmogorov [-@kolmogorov1931] showed that equation 7 can be generalized to
more complex discrete state space models than the two state model (one of which
is absorbing) introduced in the previous section:
$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial t} = P(t) Q(t) \tag{9}
$$
The system of equations is known as the *Kolmogorov forward equations*. Their
solution, in matrix form, provides a generalized method to compute the
transition probability matrix, $P(t;s)$, from the transition rate matrix,
$Q(t)$. Equation 9 is equivalent to equation 1, generalized for multiple states.
Their solution [@welton2005] is given in equation 10.
$$
P(t;s) = e ^ {tQ(t)} = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \frac{t^n}{n!}Q^n \tag{10}
$$
If the transition rates between states are known, and expressed as a matrix,
then - provided the exponential of the matrix can be found - equation 10 allows
the transition probability matrix, $P(t;s)$ to be computed, and used in
equation 6 to calculate state populations after a time cycle.

Matrix $P(t;s)$ has the property that the sum of each of its rows is one;
subjects must either leave, or stay, in each state. $Q(t)$ has the property that
the sum of each of its rows is zero; this arises from the constraint that
subjects cannot be created, or removed, from the population.

Consider the example of the two health state model discussed previously. Writing
the transition rate from *a* to *b* as $r$, and assuming that state *b* is
absorbing, then the transition rate matrix is:
$$
Q(t) = \begin{bmatrix}-r & r\\0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$
The upper left value (transition rate from *a* to *a*) is $-r$ to ensure that
the row sum is zero. Then, as expected:
$$
\begin{align*}
P(t;s) &= 
\frac{t^0}{0!}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & 1\end{bmatrix} +
\frac{t^1}{1!}\begin{bmatrix}-r & r\\0 & 0\end{bmatrix} + 
\frac{t^2}{2!}\begin{bmatrix}r^2 & -r^2\\0 & 0\end{bmatrix} + 
\frac{t^3}{3!}\begin{bmatrix}-r^3 & r^3\\0 & 0\end{bmatrix} + \:
\dots\\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
1 + (-rt) + \frac{(-rt)^2}{2!} + \frac{(-rt)^3}{3!} + \dots &
0 - (-rt) - \frac{(-rt)^2}{2!} - \frac{(-rt)^3}{3!} + \dots\\
0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}\\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
e^{-rt} & 1 - e^{-rt}\\0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\end{align*}
$$
Welton and Ades [@welton2005], for example, provide analytical solutions for a
two health state model with transitions in both directions, and for a three
health state model with one absorbing state. But in general, equation 10 is
solved numerically. For example, R package `expm` [@goulet2021] provides
methods for computing the exponential of square matrices.

## Multiple transitions per cycle

If the duration of a time cycle, $t$, is greater than zero, and finite, there
is the possibility that a subject may make more than one transition between
states in a single cycle. Certain configurations of the health states may
preclude this, for example two health states of which one is absorbing. But, in
general, the transition probability matrix should allow for this possibility. 

Consider the three health state model of figure 3. Health state *c* is an
absorbing state and there is no directly allowable transition from health
state *a* to health state *c*.

```{r}
#| fig.align = "center",
#| fig.cap = "Figure 3. A three health state model"
local({
  g <- DiagrammeR::create_graph()
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_node(graph = g, label = "a")
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_node(graph = g, label = "b")
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_node(graph = g, label = "c")
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_edge(
    graph = g,
    from = "a",
    to = "a"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_edge(
    graph = g,
    from = "a",
    to = "b"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_edge(
    graph = g,
    from = "b",
    to = "b"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_edge(
    graph = g,
    from = "b",
    to = "c"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_edge(
    graph = g,
    from = "c",
    to = "c"
  )
  # get the node ids
  nodes <- DiagrammeR::get_node_attrs(g, node_attr = "label")
  na <- which(nodes == "a")
  nb <- which(nodes == "b")
  nc <- which(nodes == "c")
  # set layout
  g <- DiagrammeR::set_node_position(g, node = na, x = 1L, y = 1L)
  g <- DiagrammeR::set_node_position(g, node = nb, x = 2L, y = 1L)
  g <- DiagrammeR::set_node_position(g, node = nc, x = 3L, y = 1L)
  # set global attributes
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "fontsize",
    value = 8L,
    attr_type = "node"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "shape",
    value = "circle",
    attr_type = "node"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "color",
    value = "black",
    attr_type = "node"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "fillcolor",
    value = "white",
    attr_type = "node"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "fontcolor",
    value = "black",
    attr_type = "node"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "color",
    value = "black",
    attr_type = "edge"
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::add_global_graph_attrs(
    g,
    attr = "penwidth",
    value = 0.5,
    attr_type = "edge"
  )
  # set loop directions
  g <- DiagrammeR::set_edge_attrs(
    g,
    edge_attr = "headport",
    values = "s",
    from = na,
    to = na
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::set_edge_attrs(
    g,
    edge_attr = "tailport",
    values = "s",
    from = na,
    to = na
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::set_edge_attrs(
    g,
    edge_attr = "headport",
    values = "s",
    from = nb,
    to = nb
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::set_edge_attrs(
    g,
    edge_attr = "tailport",
    values = "s",
    from = nb,
    to = nb
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::set_edge_attrs(
    g,
    edge_attr = "headport",
    values = "s",
    from = nc,
    to = nc
  )
  g <- DiagrammeR::set_edge_attrs(
    g,
    edge_attr = "tailport",
    values = "s",
    from = nc,
    to = nc
  )
  # name of SVG file
  svgfile <- tempfile(fileext = ".svg")
  # render it as an svg file
  DiagrammeR::export_graph(
    g,
    file_name = svgfile,
    file_type = "svg",
    width = 480L
  )
  knitr::include_graphics(path = svgfile, rel_path = FALSE)
})
```

Defining the transition rates between health states *a* and *b*, and between
*b* and *c* as $r_1$ and $r_2$ respectively, the transition rate matrix is:
$$
Q(t) = \begin{bmatrix}
-r_1 & r_1 & 0\\
0 & -r_2 & r_2\\
0 & 0 & 0\\
\end{bmatrix}
$$
From Walton and Ades' analytical solution [-@welton2005], the transition
probability matrix is:
$$
P(t; s) = \begin{bmatrix}
e^{-r_1t} &
\frac{r_1 e^{-r_2t}(1 - e^{-(r_1-r_2)t})}{r_1 - r_2} &
1 - e^{-r_1t} - \frac{r_1 e^{-r_2t}(1 - e^{-(r_1-r_2)t})}{r_1 - r_2}\\
0 & e^{-r_2t} & 1 - e^{r_2t}\\
0 & 0 & 1\\
\end{bmatrix}
$$
The probability of starting a cycle in state *b* and finishing in state *c*,
and vice-versa is identical to the model with two health states (of which one
is absorbing) which was introduced earlier; the lower right 2x2 submatrix
of $P(t; s)$ is as expected from the previous result. The top row, which
represents the probabilities of starting in health state *a*, demonstrates the
effect of multiple transitions. The population remaining in health state *a* is
as expected from previous calculations, but the probability of finishing the
cycle in either health state *b* or *c* includes the possibility that subjects
moved from *a* to *b* and then to *c* within the cycle. For example, the matrix
element in the top right is non zero, although there is no direct transition
from *a* to *c*.

Numerically, assume that 50 out of every 100 subjects in health state *a*
are at risk of a transition to health state *b* within one year ($r_1$ = 0.5),
and that 20 out of every 100 subjects in health state *b* are at risk of
transition to health state *c* within one year ($r_2$ = 0.2).

```{r}
qm <- matrix(
  c(-0.5, 0.5, 0.0, 0.0, -0.2, 0.2, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0), nrow = 3L, byrow = TRUE
)
pt <- expm::expm(x = qm)
```

$$
Q(t) = \begin{bmatrix}
`r qm[[1L, 1L]]` & `r qm[[1L, 2L]]` & `r qm[[1L, 3L]]`\\
`r qm[[2L, 1L]]` & `r qm[[2L, 2L]]` & `r qm[[2L, 3L]]`\\
`r qm[[3L, 1L]]` & `r qm[[3L, 2L]]` & `r qm[[3L, 3L]]`\\
\end{bmatrix}, \quad
P(t;s) = \begin{bmatrix}
`r pt[[1L, 1L]]` & `r pt[[1L, 2L]]` & `r pt[[1L, 3L]]`\\
`r pt[[2L, 1L]]` & `r pt[[2L, 2L]]` & `r pt[[2L, 3L]]`\\
`r pt[[3L, 1L]]` & `r pt[[3L, 2L]]` & `r pt[[3L, 3L]]`\\
\end{bmatrix}
$$
